The A–Z of Places

About this edition

Each street address was run through the U.S. Census geocoder and placed inside its city, unincorporated community and neighborhood boundary. Businesses were matched against the City of Los Angeles business registry, and landmarks against the Historic-Cultural Monument, National Register and California historic-resource lists.

About 1,400 entries were then researched one by one on the web: whether the place is still there, whether it has a new name, and where it really is. Every proposed change went to the author for a yes or no before it went in.

A “Now” note in italics says what has changed since the place was written up.

How to read an entry
  1. Name, then the NEIGHBORHOOD OR CITY and the entry’s book number.
  2. The address opens in Google Maps. Locator marks cross streets or an area where there is no street number.
  3. ClosedRenamedProbably closed lead the Now note.

Set in Newsreader and Overpass. Overpass is a free typeface drawn from Highway Gothic, the lettering on American freeway signs.
